0.long_answer: Robert Hooke was the first to observe cells in 1665 when he examined a thin slice of cork taken from the bark of a cork oak tree. He described the tiny, box-like structures that resembled the small rooms (cells) used by monks, which led to the modern term ‘cell’. Cork, as a part of a plant, is an organ not present in mammals.

1.long_answer: Robert Hooke was the first to observe the small, box-like structures in cork when he examined it under a microscope. In his work, he described these structures as 'cells' because they resembled the small rooms in a monastery. The cells he observed were the dead, air-filled cells of cork tissue, which form a protective, insulating layer in plants. Although these specific cork cells are not found in mammals, they provided the early evidence for the cellular nature of living organisms.

2.long_answer: Chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) is a clonal disorder of the hematopoietic stem cell, characterized by the expression of the BCR-ABL fusion protein, a constitutively active tyrosine kinase. Although most leukemic cells in CML show high levels of BCR-ABL, research has identified a subset of cells—thought to include leukemic stem cells—where expression of this tyrosine kinase is lower than usual. This lower level is believed to contribute to their quiescence and resistance to therapies that target rapidly dividing cells.
